Smallest event count that gives a signal

Source: R/signal_count.R
signal_count.Rd

For each number of subjects (or exposure), finds the smallest blinded event count for which the posterior probability exceeds cutoff. Plotted against the number of subjects, these counts are the boundaries of Ball and Schnell (2016, Figure 1) and the control charts of Gould and Wang (2017, Figure 2 and Table III).

Usage

signal_count(
  n,
  method = c("canary", "binbeta"),
  ...,
  cutoff = 0.95,
  y_max = NULL
)

Arguments

n

Numbers of subjects (or exposures for the Poisson likelihood of canary_post).

method

"canary" (canary_post) or "binbeta" (binbeta_post).

...

Further arguments of the posterior function (priors, k, critical values); y, n, cutoff and details are set here.

cutoff

Posterior probability threshold for a signal.

y_max

Largest count to consider; by default n (rounded down). It must be given for the Poisson likelihood.

Value

A data frame with columns n, y_crit (the smallest count with a signal, NA if none of the evaluated counts up to y_max gives one), prob (the posterior probability at y_crit, or at y_max if y_crit is NA) and prob_below (at y_crit - 1, NA if y_crit is 0).

Details

The posterior probability increases with the event count up to the first count with a signal, but not necessarily beyond it: when the event probabilities are bounded (binomial likelihood), counts near n imply event probabilities near 1 in both arms, and the probability of a large ratio falls again. The counts 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (up to y_max) are therefore evaluated until the first one with a signal, and the smallest count with a signal is found by bisection between that count and the one before it. A signal at count \(y\) means prob > cutoff, the rule of all functions of the package; Gould and Wang (2017) use \(\ge\), which differs only when the probability equals cutoff exactly. The largest acceptable count of Ball and Schnell (2016) is the result minus 1.

References

Ball, G. and Schnell, P. M. (2016). Blinded safety signal monitoring for the FDA IND reporting final rule. In J. Lin et al. (eds.), Statistical Applications from Clinical Trials and Personalized Medicine to Finance and Business Analytics, ICSA Book Series in Statistics, 201–209. Springer, Cham. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-42568-9_17

Gould, A. L. and Wang, W. B. (2017). Monitoring potential adverse event rate differences using data from blinded trials: the canary in the coal mine. Statistics in Medicine, 36(1), 92–104. doi:10.1002/sim.7129

See also

count_oc

Examples

# Gould and Wang (2017), Table III: control prior Beta(20, 980), signal if
# P(R > 1) > 0.8
signal_count(n = 100, method = "canary", prior_c = c(20, 980),
             cutoff = 0.8)
#>     n y_crit      prob prob_below
#> 1 100      6 0.8421326  0.7167684
